newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST-UK PSBR seen at 1.0 bln stg in December.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-UK PSBR seen at 1.0 bln stg in December.

text.p: The British government's budget deficit in December is seen almost double last year's 0.6 billion sterling, inflated largely by an extra one billion pounds paid in interest on strippable gilts, economists said on Wednesday.

According to a Reuter survey, economists expect the public sector borrowing requirement (PSBR) to be 1.0 billion stg in December. This would leave a cumulative PSBR for the year to date of 18.8 billion pounds, some 4.3 billion lower than the same time last year.

"Privatisation proceeds are expected to be around 250 million sterling in December, but offsetting that are increased interest payments on strippable gilts triggered by the reform of the gilt market," said Daiwa economist Katy Peters.
She is more pessimistic than the consensus, forecasting a 1.8 billion stg defict in December, down from November's 2.6 billion.
But HSBC Markets economist Jonathan Loynes was rather more upbeat, expecting a slight acceleration in receipts growth to 6.5 percent in December, mainly due to a rebound in income tax receipts.

"On the spending side, we expect a slight slowdown in the growth of departmental spending to just below three percent after the pick-up in recent months," he said, adding total spending would be pushed up by the one billion in interest payments.
Loynes expects the PSBR to be 1.2 billion in December, giving 1.5 billion stg excluding privatisation receipts.
Ciaran Barr from Deutsche Morgan Grenfell was also fairly optimistic.

"The PSBR looks set to undershoot the government's full year forecast of 26.4 billion sterling," he said. "Receipts growth is running comfortably ahead of government forecasts while the overshoot in government spending seems to be falling."
But Peters said strong spending would jeopardise the government's chances of hitting its target.

"I don't think it will achieve its target. The bit that really worries me is the expenditure side, I don't think the government is controlling it sufficiently well to hit the target," she said, adding a lot of departmental spending often occurs around March.
Loynes also said total spending was set to overshoot the official forecast by several billion pounds this year.
"But any recent disappointment on the spending side of the accounts has been offset by the performance of tax receipts, where growth has turned decisively upwards," he said.
He did sound a note of caution on corporation tax receipts, which have been particularly strong.

"This may reflect the fact payments at this time of year tend to be dominated by the buoyant financial sector," he said. "The next few months, when manufacturers will pay their bills, could see a weaker picture."
Peters said signs of weaker than expected retail sales in December could lead to lower VAT receipts.
